units.translation: [The Attic form dei is preserved more frequently in the manuscripts of Aristophanes than in those of the tragedians, in which αἰεί [always] is very often written, and likewise in compounds, sometimes even against the meter: from which it follows that there is no authority of the books in this matter. For scribes accustomed to the Homeric reading introduced αἰεί [always] not only into the scenic poets, but also into prose writers both old and recent, for whom dei has now generally been restored from older manuscripts, not even excepting Thucydides, whom Marcellinus, the writer of his life, following the authority of his manuscript, believed to have preferred αἰεί [always], ὡς ἐπὶ πλεῖστον δὲ χρῆται τῇ ἀρχαίᾳ Ἀτθίδι, ὅταν τὴν δίφθογγον τὴν αἱ ἀντὶ τοῦ α γράφη, αἰεί λέγων [and he uses the ancient Attic for the most part, whenever he writes the diphthong ai instead of a, saying aiei], to which opinion not even the surviving manuscripts are favorable, of which the best and oldest fairly consistently offer ἀεί [always], which is not likely to have been introduced by scribes. As to the measure, there is no doubt that Apollonius in his book on adverbs (in Bekker's Anecdota p. 600), where he discusses the change of a into long ā, rightly judged ἀναλογώτερον [more analogical] to be ἀεί [always] with long ā. In the everyday speech of the Athenians, however, dei seems never to have been pronounced otherwise than with short a, and this measure was already sometimes used by the epic poets where the meter would not admit the form αἰεί [always] proper to the epic dialect, as in Homer Il. 12, 211 Εκτορ, ἀεὶ μέν πως — [Hector, always somehow —]. But the Attic poets, who did not use the epic and Ionic αἰεί [always], said dei sometimes with short a, sometimes with long, as was convenient for the meter: whence very many examples of both measures are found in the scenic poets.] which is said either of uninterrupted time or has the meaning of the adverb ἑκάστοτε [each time], which grammarians are accustomed to explain by ἀεί [always].
which Schneider in his Lexicon preferred to write ἀείξενον [always hostile to strangers].
if it was correctly corrected by Dobree from what is read in Athenaeus 15 p. 667e κότταβος ἀεί [kottabos always].
i.e., τὸν ἑκάστοτε κρατοῦντα [the one ruling at each time], each one ruling at each time, although ἀεί [always] in this sense is generally placed between the article and the noun.
The epic form aiév the tragedians do not use except when the meter demands it: on which I have spoken in Lex. Soph. p. 7a.
But wrongly at Sept. 857 πίτυλον, ὃς αἰὲν δι᾿ Αχέροντ' ἀμείβεται [the oar-stroke, which ever passes through Acheron], where dei should be written.
Always the pain of the present evil will wear you down.
Always indeed you are pitiless and full of boldness.
But he, ever wrathful, set an unbending mind.
For what is fated for Zeus except to rule always?
For always nightly visions – they were comforting.
To the lord, faith first of all always.
For always it is youth for the old to learn well.
A resident alien for all time, always a stranger,
You lie always on the ground.
And for the future there will be – always this council of judges.
